tagline.text: An evening street market in downtown Davao with grilled food and massages

location.label: Location
location.text: M. Roxas Avenue, Poblacion District, Davao City (near Ateneo de Davao University)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (the November–April dry season is the most comfortable; rain can affect the stalls)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,200 (meals, massage and snacks, per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: About 30–45 minutes by car from Francisco Bangoy International Airport (DVO)

children.text: Roxas Night Market is an evening stall market on Roxas Avenue in downtown Davao. Charcoal-grilled food and seafood, secondhand and ready-to-wear clothes, accessories and roadside massages share one street, giving you a close look at how Davao people spend their evenings.

Roxas Night Market is held on M. Roxas Avenue in the Poblacion District of Davao City. OpenStreetMap lists it as a marketplace at about 7.0704°N, 125.6134°E, very close to Ateneo de Davao University. The market takes the form of tented stalls lined up along the road. It is divided roughly into food, ready-to-wear and secondhand clothes (ukay-ukay), accessories and massage, and after sunset people gather and the street turns into an evening bazaar. There is no entrance fee, and paying cash at each stall is the norm.

Its history has had some ups and downs. In August 2016 the Davao mayor ordered the market, then three years old, closed for violating city rules, and MindaNews reported that about 700 vendors were affected. SunStar reported that on September 2, 2016 a bombing at the market killed 17 people and wounded 69. The market continued afterward, with security reportedly strengthened. Since then the city has run it by raffling vendor spots in three-month terms, and a 2019 article estimated about 3,000 visitors a day. City figures put the market's revenue at about ₱2.24 million in 2014 and about ₱5.47 million in 2015. One food-vendor couple said they moved to Roxas Avenue from San Pedro Street in 2013, which shows how quickly the market grew in a short time.

The COVID-19 pandemic shut the market for a while. It reopened on September 12, 2020 at 25 percent capacity, but curfews sharply shortened its hours, and it returned to its usual form on March 24, 2022. According to the Davao city government, at least 286 vendors came back at that time: 56 food vendors, 65 ready-to-wear vendors, 65 accessories vendors and 100 massage therapists. One visitor's account the same year counted about 86 tented food stalls, so the number of stalls appears to vary from time to time.

The market is presented as a place to see Davao's daily life and food all at once. A 2019 article says one three-month term accommodated 130 accessories vendors, 130 ready-to-wear vendors, 116 food vendors and more than 100 massage therapists, which gives a sense of its scale. The city has since discussed extending the market toward Quezon Boulevard and opening more night markets across the city's three districts. The mix of stalls, operating hours and security-check rules have changed over the years, though. This guide gathers articles and reviews from 2019 to 2025, so check recent news before you go.

A 2025 visitor's account mentions seafood such as cuttlefish, catfish, and tuna belly and panga, as well as sausages, silog meals, waffles and corndogs. Reviews say you can have light snacks or a hearty meal.
Shakes made from green and ripe mango, watermelon, papaya and pineapple, fruit on sticks and coconut water stand out. "Dirty ice cream" is also a popular dessert.

A 2022 review says more than 70 massage providers line the road. Records give about ₱300 for a full-body massage, about ₱100 for the back or feet, about ₱70 for the hands or head, and about ₱50 for a dry massage, but confirm current prices locally.

Reviews say about 90 stalls sold phone accessories, hats, keychains, earrings and wallets. A service of writing your name on a keychain is also reported. It is a good place to pick up light Davao souvenirs.
One account says about 90 stalls sold ready-to-wear clothes for all ages, bags and shoes, and that it has a secondhand-market feel that invites slow browsing.
Reviews say it is within walking distance of hotels in downtown Davao. One visitor said it was about a 10-minute walk from their lodging.
Reviews say the market has four entrances and that military and police personnel are stationed around it. Given the strong security, you must follow the bag rules.

items.subtitle: Arrive, eat, walk and finish with a massage

items.title: Combining with a Davao itinerary
items.subtitle: City sights by day, the night market in the evening

children.text: Visit churches and museums in downtown Davao, or make a trip to a nature spot nearby.
Rest at your hotel, then walk to the night market for dinner.
Fly from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to Francisco Bangoy International Airport (DVO) in Davao. Check airline notices for routes and timetables.

Take a taxi, a ride-hailing car or a jeepney to Roxas Avenue. Check jeepney routes locally.

10 minutes

Traffic around the market is heavy in the evening, so it is quicker to get into and out of a taxi or ride-hailing car on a street a little way from the market entrance.

items.title: By rental car or private car

children.text: The roads around the market are congested, so it is better to park in a nearby lot or your hotel's parking and walk.
There are plans to bring food trucks to the Roxas segment near Quezon Boulevard, so road conditions may change. Check beforehand.

Roxas Night Market is an outdoor stall market, so weather affects it, but it basically opens all year. Davao is relatively outside the typhoon paths in the Philippines, though showers are common. Around the November–April dry season is the most comfortable for walking.
The hours are in the evening. Sources differ, giving the opening time as

or
, so check each time you go. Weekend evenings and holidays are the busiest, so to enjoy it quietly, an early weekday evening is best.

During COVID, hours were once cut to 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. because of curfews. That is unlikely to happen again, but hours can change temporarily depending on events or the security situation. During Davao's big festivals in particular, traffic downtown can be controlled on some days, so decide beforehand on the route you can walk from your lodging and your transport home.

It is convenient to stay in central downtown Davao. Many hotels near Roxas Night Market are within walking distance, according to many reviews. The road in front of the market can be noisy, so consider noise when choosing a room.

Meals are usually taken at the night market's stalls. Charcoal-grilled chicken, pork and seafood are the core, along with sausages, waffles, corndogs and fruit on sticks. There are said to be halal stalls too, and Korean street food. If you worry about hygiene, pick stalls with a long line or where the cooking is done in front of you. You can also sit down to eat at restaurants beside the market building.

For first-time visitors I suggest this order. First walk the street from one end to the other to see the food and the layout of the zones, remember the stalls you like, and buy on the way back. The tables under the tents are close to the food zone, so seats are easy to find, and a massage at the very end of your walk loosens tired legs. On weekends there are many people, so set a meeting point so you do not get separated from your group. English, Tagalog and Bisaya are mixed in conversation with local vendors, so it is easy to confirm prices with your fingers or a phone calculator.
Most stalls accept cash only, so carry plenty of small bills and use an ATM beforehand.
A 2022 review says backpacks, even empty ones, were not allowed in. A small crossbody bag, or leaving your bag at the hotel, is safer.
Agree on the price before you get a massage.
The clothing zone takes time to browse, so allow some leeway.
Check how seafood and grilled food are cooked yourself, and if your stomach is sensitive, try things slowly.
Pickpockets can operate in the evening, so keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
Hours and security rules can change, so check recent news before you leave.
When traveling at night, use a ride-hailing car or a regular taxi.
According to one visitor's account, buildings near the market also have restaurants and eateries, so you can sit and eat there if the stalls are not to your taste.
The night market is a security zone with military and police personnel stationed. Cooperate with bag checks and follow rules such as those on carrying bags.
The market was the site of a bombing on September 2, 2016, so security checks are fairly strong. Follow the latest rules.
Beware of pickpockets and loss at crowded times.
Hygiene at stalls varies from one to the next, so look at the cooking conditions.
Operating hours may change from time to time, so confirm them before you leave.
Stalls may decrease or roads may be closed because of rain or events.
The night market is in the center of Davao City. Sightseeing, restaurants and shopping are clustered close by.
